frames.narration: Illustration with round numbers: someone posts an @everyone announcement in a very large channel, and in the next few seconds many people open the app. Each reader's app asks for the newest messages in that one channel. Every request reaches the API monolith first.

The API calls the data service with a routing key. For messages the key is the channel ID, and consistent hash-based routing sends every request with the same key to the same instance. That is what lets one instance see all the readers of the channel at once.
The first request for this row makes the instance start a worker task. The worker queries the database for the partition of channel 41 and the current time bucket.
Requests that arrive while the read is running find the existing task and subscribe to it. They do not query the database themselves, so the database sees one read however many readers join.
The database returns the row. The worker hands the same result to every subscriber, and the service answers all the waiting API calls.

The API returns the messages to the readers. A reader who scrolls back far enough asks for an older time bucket, which is a different partition, and goes through the same path. Without the data service, the same crowd would have sent every read straight to the node that holds this partition.
